candidates.locator: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration: VIII. The Person of Christ, ¶64–66
candidates.phrase: one divine omnipotence, power, majesty, and glory, which is peculiar to the divine nature alone
candidates.rationale: The Formula of Concord states that glory, with omnipotence, power, and majesty, is peculiar to the divine nature alone, affirming glory as a property proper to divinity itself, distinct from the assumed human nature.
candidates.chunk_text: We, therefore, hold and teach, in conformity with the ancient orthodox Church, as it has explained this doctrine from the Scriptures, that the human nature in Christ has received this majesty according to the manner of the personal union, namely, because the entire fulness of the divinity dwells in Christ, not as in other holy men or angels, but bodily, as in its own body, so that it shines forth with all its majesty, power, glory, and efficacy in the assumed human nature, voluntarily when and as He [Christ] wills, and in, with, and through the same manifests, exercises, and executes His divine power, glory, and efficacy, as the soul does in the body and fire in glowing iron (for by means of these illustrations, as was also mentioned above, the entire ancient Church has explained this doctrine). This was concealed and withheld [for the greater part] at the time of the humiliation; but now, after the form of a servant [or exinanition] has been laid aside, it is fully, powerfully, and publicly exercised before all saints, in heaven and on earth; and in the life to come we shall also behold this His glory face to face, John 17:24. Thus there is and remains in Christ only one divine omnipotence, power, majesty, and glory, which is peculiar to the divine nature alone; but it shines, manifests, and exercises itself fully, yet voluntarily, in, with, and through the assumed, exalted human nature in Christ. Just as in glowing iron there are not two kinds of power to shine and burn [as though the fire had a peculiar, and the iron also a peculiar and separate power of shining and burning], but the power to shine and to burn is a property of the fire; but since the fire is united with the iron, it manifests and exercises this its power to shine and to burn in, with, and through the glowing iron, so that thence and from this union also the glowing iron has the power to shine and to burn without conversion of the essence and of the natural properties of fire and iron.

opus.grammatical_subject: "one divine omnipotence, power, majesty, and glory" (with the relative clause predicating it as "peculiar to the divine nature alone")
opus.speech_act_note: The Declaration speaks in its own voice ("We, therefore, hold and teach... Thus there is and remains"); it is a positive doctrinal assertion, not a report of an opponent's view.
opus.floor_reason: The passage states that the one omnipotence, power, majesty, and glory is "peculiar to the divine nature alone," which affirms glory as properly and exclusively divine.
opus.reason: Phrase is verbatim; the standard asserts in its own voice that glory belongs properly to the divine nature alone, meeting the floor of glory as properly divine. The surrounding christological context (the assumed human nature shining with divine majesty) does not shift the subject of the quoted clause, though it should be read as distinguishing, not transferring, the divine property.
